# Diagnosing a Flat Battery: Why Charging Fails After Months of Inactivity

When a car battery sits dead for four months, the immediate assumption is often simple neglect or a parasitic drain from an interior light left on. However, the symptom you described—where the vehicle refuses to engage door locks even after a brief 20km drive—suggests something more complex than just a depleted chemical state. You are likely dealing with **deep discharge damage** combined with a potential charging system failure, not merely a battery that needs a top-up.

### The Physics of Deep Discharge and Sulfation

Lithium-ion batteries in electronics suffer from degradation when left at 0% for extended periods; lead-acid automotive batteries face a similar, albeit chemically distinct, enemy called **sulfation**. When a lead-acid battery drops below its minimum voltage threshold (typically around 10.5V to 11V) and sits there for weeks or months, lead sulfate crystals form on the plates.

Over time, these crystals harden into large, insoluble structures that prevent the electrochemical reaction required to store energy. Even if you can force a current back into the battery using an external charger, the internal resistance remains so high that it cannot accept a charge efficiently. This manifests exactly as your car does: the engine cranks because the starter motor draws a massive surge of current momentarily, but once the load is removed, the voltage collapses instantly because the plates can no longer hold a charge.

The fact that you drove 20km might actually be worse than doing nothing. While driving generates electricity via the alternator, if the battery was already sulfated to this degree, it likely drew power from the alternator without being able to store any of it. The alternator works by spinning a rotor to create a magnetic field that induces current in the stator; however, if the battery's internal resistance is too high (due to sulfation), the voltage regulator may interpret this as a fault and stop charging output entirely to protect the system, or simply fail to push enough amps into the dead cells.

### Diagnosing the Alternator vs. The Battery

Before you spend money on a new battery, you must verify whether the alternator is functioning correctly. A common pitfall in these scenarios is assuming the battery is bad because it won't hold a charge, when in reality, the alternator stopped charging months ago due to heat or age.

You can perform a quick diagnostic using a multimeter:
1.  **Measure resting voltage** with the engine off. If it reads below 12V, the battery is deeply discharged.
2.  **Start the engine and measure again.** A healthy alternator should boost this to between 13.8V and 14.7V immediately.
3.  **Monitor under load.** Turn on all accessories (headlights, AC, radio). If the voltage drops below 13V or spikes above 15V, the voltage regulator is failing.

If the alternator output is normal but the battery still won't hold a charge after sitting overnight, the sulfation is irreversible. Standard trickle chargers often cannot overcome the high internal resistance of a fully sulfated plate; they simply waste energy heating up the electrolyte without restoring capacity. In this case, attempting to "revive" it at a local shop with their specific equipment might yield temporary results, but the battery will likely fail again within days or weeks.

### Preventing Future Failures: The Smart Battery Disconnect

The root cause of your situation was almost certainly **parasitic drain**. Modern vehicles have complex electronics that draw small amounts of current even when parked to maintain security systems, memory settings, and clock accuracy. A typical draw is 50mA (milliamps). Left on for four months, this consumes roughly 18Ah of capacity. Most batteries are rated at 40–60Ah, meaning a single bad light can kill the charge in under three weeks if not monitored.

To avoid repeating this specific failure mode, consider installing a **smart battery disconnect relay** or using a smart charger with an auto-shutoff feature that monitors voltage. Alternatively, a manual battery tender (trickle charger) plugged into an outlet is essential for vehicles stored long-term during summer months when temperature fluctuations accelerate chemical reactions inside the battery.

If your diagnostics confirm the alternator is working but the battery is physically dead due to sulfation, replacing it is the only reliable solution. While online forums often debate DIY fixes, in automotive electrical engineering, a battery that cannot accept a charge after deep discharge is considered end-of-life hardware. Ignoring this can lead to further damage to your vehicle's voltage regulator or starter motor due to inconsistent power delivery.
